title: Christian beginnings: Acts and the early witnesses
summary: The account in Acts provides the Christian beginnings to which later Anabaptist communities looked for their understanding of discipleship, baptism, and shared life.
paragraphs: The New Testament account of the first Christian communities stands at the beginning of this timeline. Its descriptions of baptism, fellowship, care for neighbours, and witness helped shape later Anabaptist readings of the church.

Martyrs’ Mirror reaches back to the early church to tell a story of faithful witness. These early Christians were not members of the sixteenth-century Anabaptist movement. The book’s claims about continuity belong to its historical and theological interpretation and should be read as such.

title: The Zürich baptisms

date.basis: Date of the event or documented activity; see cited sources

summary: On 21 January 1525, Conrad Grebel baptized George Blaurock at a gathering associated with Felix Manz in Zürich. This is a central starting point for Swiss Anabaptist history.
paragraphs: A circle of reform-minded Christians in Zürich came to believe that baptism should follow a person’s own confession of faith. Their disagreement with the city’s religious settlement brought pressure to conform.

On 21 January 1525, Conrad Grebel baptized George Blaurock, and others at the gathering were then baptized. The event became a defining beginning for the Swiss Brethren. Anabaptism also developed in other regions, so the wider story includes several centres and traditions.

title: Felix Manz and the cost of conviction

date.basis: Date of the event or documented activity; see cited sources

summary: Felix Manz was drowned in Zürich on 5 January 1527. His story is central to the memory of persecution among the Swiss Brethren.
paragraphs: Felix Manz was one of the early Zürich advocates of believers’ baptism. He was executed by drowning in the Limmat on 5 January 1527.

The supplied Martyrs’ Mirror heading gives 1526 for Felix Mantz. That heading is preserved on the source page; this overview uses the date given in the later reference. Keeping both visible allows readers to examine the difference.

title: The Schleitheim Articles

date.basis: Date of the event or documented activity; see cited sources

summary: The Schleitheim Articles set out seven points of agreement for a gathered Anabaptist community, including baptism, communion, church discipline, and refusal of the sword.
paragraphs: The 1527 Schleitheim Articles were written as a document of union. They are associated with Michael Sattler and the Swiss Brethren.

The articles address baptism, the ban, breaking of bread, separation, shepherds, the sword, and oaths. They help readers understand a form of Anabaptist discipleship while leaving room to investigate differences among other early groups.

title: Preserving the memory: Martyrs’ Mirror

date.basis: Date of the event or documented activity; see cited sources

summary: Thieleman J. van Braght’s collection preserved accounts of Christian witnesses and Anabaptist martyrs, along with letters, confessions, and reflections.
paragraphs: Martyrs’ Mirror brings together a large collection of accounts spanning Christian beginnings and the persecution of Anabaptists. It preserves letters and testimonies as well as narrative accounts.

The book is a historical source with its own theological purpose. This archive preserves the supplied text, makes its sections searchable, and connects each section to the intact edition rather than silently rewriting its language or dates.

title: The Schwarzenau Brethren

date.basis: Date of the event or documented activity; see cited sources

summary: A group baptized in the Eder River at Schwarzenau began a movement shaped by both Anabaptist convictions and Pietism.
paragraphs: In August 1708, five men and three women gathered for baptism at the Eder River in Schwarzenau. Their movement combined influences from Anabaptism and Pietism.
This related history belongs in the wider timeline without treating every Brethren body as identical to the Mennonite, Amish, or Hutterite traditions.

title: Anabaptist history is still being written
summary: The present-day story includes communities across continents and many different traditions. Local histories, migrations, mission, and relationships between churches are part of the record still being gathered.
paragraphs: This site is an open historical archive for the wider Anabaptist family. It does not assume that one branch represents every community or that all relationships can be drawn as a simple line.

Modern history grows through documented contributions. Congregational records, dated testimonies, archive materials, and clearly credited photographs can help explain the people and events beyond the supplied timeline.
